findings.paper_title: Report No.84.2026 - Q1 2026-27 Finance Report
findings.headline: £1.217m of savings plans rated RED: forecast to fall short of target by over 25% with limited mitigation scope
findings.detail: Of the £6.563m medium-term savings target, four plans totalling £1.217m are rated RED as forecast to fall short by over 25% with limited mitigation. These include garden waste (subscription numbers below budget despite price increase), planning budget realignment (now dependent on delayed/reduced-recovery planning reform), highways and transport realignment (service forecasting overspends not savings), and DRT additional contributions (funding gap remains).
findings.matters: Multiple budgeted savings plans are failing to materialise. Combined with the Q1 overspend, this suggests the council is struggling to manage emerging cost and demand pressures and has hedged its budget on income/savings assumptions that are proving unreliable.
findings.figures: £1.217m in red-rated savings plans out of £6.563m total savings target; only £5.9m forecast achieved (89.9%)
findings.quote: Some savings remain at risk, notably those linked to planning fee reforms, transport services and additional income generation proposals.

findings.paper_title: Report No.84.2026 - Q1 2026-27 Finance Report
findings.headline: Melton Local Regeneration Fund capital scheme slipping £2.3m due to contractor cost overruns requiring value engineering
findings.detail: The Melton LRF project (part of a £12.182m total LRF commitment) is forecast to slip £2.3m into future years. Slippage is driven by ongoing work to finalise construction affordability following contractor estimates that exceeded available budget. Key project dependencies including planning, access, lease arrangements and procurement approvals remain unresolved before main contract award.
findings.matters: A major capital scheme is running over budget at the design/procurement stage. Value engineering will be needed to bring costs back within available budget, and multiple project dependencies remain unresolved.
findings.figures: £2.3m slippage on £12.182m total Melton LRF project
findings.quote: The project is forecast to slip into future financial years due to ongoing work to finalise the construction affordability position, including value engineering and revisions to the delivery strategy following contractor estimates exceeding the available construction budget.

findings.paper_title: Report No.84.2026 - Q1 2026-27 Finance Report
findings.headline: Demand Responsive Transport service £0.2m funding gap with business case under review for model sustainability
findings.detail: Public Transport is forecasting a £0.2m funding gap on the DRT service. The service is developing a business case to reassess the assumptions underpinning the DRT model, with further information expected at Q2. This suggests the current operating model assumptions may not be sustainable and could require significant changes.
findings.matters: A business case review of an established service suggests current financial or operational viability concerns. This may foreshadow service redesign or reduced provision.
findings.figures: £0.2m funding gap on DRT service
findings.quote: Public Transport is currently forecasting a funding gap of £0.2m on the DRT service. The service is reviewing options to mitigate this pressure and is developing a business case to reassess the assumptions underpinning the Demand Responsive Transport (DRT) service.

findings.paper_title: Report No.84.2026 - Q1 2026-27 Finance Report
findings.headline: Dry Mixed Recycling cost pressure of £190k from contractor facility fire requiring emergency diversion
findings.detail: Dry Mixed Recycling is forecast to overspend by £190k in Q1 due to a fire at the current contractor's facility requiring material to be diverted to an alternative processing site at higher cost. This is compounded by Waste Disposal overspending by £131k from higher HWRC volumes. The council is progressing procurement and service review activity to address these pressures.
findings.matters: An operational disruption (contractor facility fire) is creating material unbudgeted costs. The council faces both this emergency pressure and structural waste volume increases, suggesting the waste service model may need restructuring.
findings.figures: £190k DMR overspend, £131k Waste Disposal overspend
findings.quote: Dry Mixed Recycling (DMR) is forecast to overspend by £190k at Quarter 1 due to higher processing costs following a fire at the current contractor's facility, requiring material to be diverted to an alternative processing site.

findings.paper_title: Report No.84.2026 - Q1 2026-27 Finance Report
findings.headline: Planning fee income reform delivering 90% cost recovery instead of 100%, starting December 2026 not April 2027
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumed full cost recovery from planning fee reforms starting April 2027. Legislation has now been confirmed at 90% cost recovery starting December 2026. This is one of four savings plans rated RED as forecast to fall short of target by over 25% with limited mitigation scope. Planning application volumes also remain subdued nationally, creating Q1 overspend of £0.2m.
findings.matters: This is a budgeted savings/income plan that is now delivering materially less than anticipated. It demonstrates income assumption risk and failed budget realisations.
findings.figures: 90% recovery instead of full cost recovery; December 2026 start instead of April 2027; £0.2m Q1 overspend
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget assumed that full cost recovery would be achieved during the second half of the year following the anticipated introduction of legislation allowing local authorities to set their own planning fees. At the point of forecast the legislation was expected to come in from April 2027. Since the forecast legislation has been confirmed at 90% of cost and will commence from December 2026.

findings.paper_title: Report No.84.2026 - Q1 2026-27 Finance Report
findings.headline: Children's placements overspending by £1.1m from single unanticipated high-cost placement
findings.detail: The placements budget is forecasting a £1.1m overspend, with a new high-cost placement that was not anticipated at budget setting driving the pressure. Additionally, the Children's Home project has slipped past its planned opening date, meaning budgeted cost avoidance and income benefits will not materialise as planned. The service is reviewing commissioning arrangements but results are uncertain.
findings.matters: Placement costs are volatile and driven by individual cases. A single unanticipated high-cost placement suggests either forecasting weakness or genuine demand volatility that cannot be predicted, creating budget risk.
findings.figures: £1.1m forecast overspend; Children's Home opening delayed beyond Q1 forecast
findings.quote: The children's placements budget is forecasting an overspend of £1.1m, primarily driven by a new high-cost placement that was not anticipated at the time the 2026/27 budget was set.

findings.paper_title: Report No.84.2026 - Q1 2026-27 Finance Report
findings.headline: £15.5m accumulated DSG deficit with no confirmed government funding for 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: The in-year Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast at £5.4m. Combined with the £10.068m brought forward, this creates a £15.452m accumulated deficit equivalent to 10.1% of the council's revised net revenue budget. The council must continue to cash-flow this deficit, but government has not confirmed how DSG deficits will be funded going forward. A recovery plan has been submitted and the council expects an announcement in autumn, but this is conditional.
findings.matters: A £15.5m contingent liability that must be cash-flowed represents a material financial risk. Dependency on future government funding decisions creates uncertainty about the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £5.4m in-year deficit forecast, £15.452m accumulated deficit, 10.1% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: Government has not yet confirmed how DSG deficits will be funded for 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Early debt repayment of £4.5m at 6.69% average rate; no new borrowing undertaken
findings.detail: The council repaid £4.5m of PWLB debt during the year at an average rate of 6.69%, with breakage costs of £0.5m, using investment balances. This reduced the debt portfolio from the budgeted position and resulted in net General Fund savings of £0.2m per annum from lower interest costs. No new borrowing was undertaken.
findings.matters: The council is actively managing down its debt position and maintaining an under-borrowed position (£4.2m under the Capital Financing Requirement). This is positive but requires sustained investment capacity.
findings.figures: £4.5m debt repayment; 6.69% average rate; £0.5m breakage costs; £0.2m net annual General Fund savings; debt portfolio £14.3m at year-end
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council repaid a further £4.5m of loan debt at an average rate of 6.69% with breakage costs of £0.5m using investment balances.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Treasury achieved 4.42% investment return vs 3.98% benchmark but dependent on £10.1m DSG deficit held in cash rather than invested
findings.detail: Strong treasury performance with £2.5m investment income (vs £2.0m budget) achieved 4.42% average return on £51.5m average investment balances. However, the council cash-flowed the £10.1m DSG accumulated deficit during the year, reducing investment balances and foregoing approximately £0.5m of interest income that would otherwise have supported council services.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is not only a spending pressure but also an opportunity cost burden, reducing available revenue from treasury activities. As the deficit grows further, this foregone income increases.
findings.figures: £2.5m investment income vs £2.0m budget; 4.42% actual vs 3.98% benchmark return; £51.5m average investment balance; £10.1m DSG held in cash; estimated £0.5m foregone interest
findings.quote: The Council has cash-flowed the accumulated deficit, which has reduced overall cash balances during the year. As a result, an average £10.1m was not available for treasury investment, leading to an estimated £0.5m reduction in interest income in 2025/26 that would otherwise have been available to support Council services.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital programme £3.1m reprofiled into future years; Highways staffing changes impacting delivery capacity
findings.detail: The council reprofiled £3.1m of capital schemes out of 2025/26 due to delivery delays. Key slippages include Highways (£1.5m overall due to senior staffing change and new Thomas Bows contract embedding), Local Regeneration Fund projects (£0.6m combined due to Anglian Water negotiations and project review), and Property services (£0.3m). Delivery plans have been reset but the slippage indicates execution risk.
findings.matters: Capital delivery slippage in a small authority often signals constrained internal capacity. The reliance on key individuals (senior Highways staff) creates implementation risk. Strategic schemes like Levelling Up Fund projects are experiencing extended timelines.
findings.figures: £3.1m total reprofiling; Highways £1.5m; Local Regeneration Fund Digital Visitor Experience £0.3m; Local Regeneration Fund Local Link £0.3m; Property £0.3m
findings.quote: The Highways service has proactively managed a period of senior staffing change, alongside embedding the new Thomas Bows contract in its first full year of operation. While this has temporarily impacted delivery capacity and contributed to slippage within the capital programme, mitigating actions have been implemented and delivery plans reset.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: SEND Reform Plan requires £360k local investment but DfE allocated only £25k; council unable to absorb structural funding gap
findings.detail: The Department for Education provided approximately £25k transformation funding for Rutland's mandatory Local SEND Reform Plan, but the council's assessment is that a prudent three-year reform programme requires £360k. Officers argue this reflects a structural issue where smaller authorities bear disproportionately higher fixed costs despite identical statutory responsibilities and demand.
findings.matters: This signals a systemic funding problem that cannot be solved locally. The council is using its Innovation Fund reserve to bridge a gap created by national policy design, which is unsustainable long-term for smaller unitaries.
findings.figures: DfE allocation £25k; Council assessed need £360k; three-year programme; all top-tier authorities have same statutory responsibilities
findings.quote: Current transformation funding for Rutland is approximately £25k, which does not reflect the scale of capacity and system change required. Officers have assessed that a prudent and deliverable programme of reform will require investment of approximately £360k over the initial three-year period.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Bed and Breakfast homelessness costs £224k over budget; actual cost £367/week but Housing Benefit subsidy capped at £90/week
findings.detail: The council is currently supporting 43 households in temporary B&B accommodation where the funding gap has increased by £167k year-on-year. The average cost is £367 per week per household but Housing Benefit subsidy is capped at £90/week. The service has partially offset this through improved recovery of overpayments, but the residual pressure remains.
findings.matters: This reflects a national trend where temporary accommodation funding gaps increased 30% in the past year. For a small unitary, this creates material unbudgeted pressure and the council is unlikely to recover the gap from subsidy changes.
findings.figures: £224k shortfall; average cost £367/week; Housing Benefit subsidy £90/week; supporting 43 households; £167k increase from prior year; national trend shows 30% gap increase
findings.quote: Housing Benefit costs for Bed and Breakfast accommodation continue to exceed Government subsidy, resulting in a £224k shortfall, an increase of £167k compared to previous years. The Council is currently supporting around 43 households (35 at Q3) in Bed and Breakfast accommodation, where Housing Benefit subsidy is capped at £90 per week against an average cost of £367 per week

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Adult Social Care older people spending £2.1m over budget; 27 additional residential care users at higher average weekly costs
findings.detail: Older People Residential Care overspent by £1.9m driven by increased demand (27 additional service users) and higher-than-budgeted average weekly costs. Additional pressures came from void costs on expanded block bed provision pending full utilisation. Working Age Adults also overspent by £348k due to rising costs and complexity of needs.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest single budget pressure. The ratio of new to departing service users remains high, indicating sustained demand growth that may not slow. This is a leading indicator of affordability risk in councils with aging populations.
findings.figures: £1.9m overspend on older people residential; £348k overspend on working age adults; 27 additional service users; working age overspend primarily in Direct Payments and Mental Health services
findings.quote: Older People Residential Care is a £1.9m overspend, driven primarily by increased demand, with 27 additional service users and higher than assumed average weekly costs. The ratio of new service users to those leaving the service has been higher than average.

findings.paper_title: Report No. 57.2026 - 2025-26 Financial Outturn Report, 09/06/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew £4.2m in-year to £10.1m accumulated, requiring 10% local funding from reserves
findings.detail: The high-needs DSG overspend is driven primarily by Education, Health and Care Plans increasing 17% in the year. While the government will cover 90% (£9.1m) via the High Needs Stability Grant from autumn 2026, the council must fund the remaining 10% (£1.0m). This remains subject to the council's Local SEND Reform Plan being approved by the Department for Education by mid-June 2026.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is structural and growing, with ongoing demand risk. The council is dependent on government grant approval and meeting reform conditions, creating future funding uncertainty.
findings.figures: £4.2m in-year overspend; £10.1m accumulated deficit; EHCPs rose 17%; 90% grant = £9.1m; 10% council contribution = £1.0m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 overspend of £4.2m has increased the accumulated deficit to £10.1m. The main driver of this overspend is the cost associated with an increase in the number of Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) which have risen 17% in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Report No.73.2026 - Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Financial Management Code assessment identifies forecasting consistency and longer-term financial planning as needing further strengthening
findings.detail: The Financial Management Code assessment accompanying the AGS demonstrates strong overall compliance with financial management standards, but identifies forecasting consistency and longer-term financial planning as areas needing further strengthening.
findings.matters: Forecasting consistency and financial planning capability are central to assessing whether a council can reliably project its financial position and meet future obligations.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The Financial Management Code assessment demonstrates strong compliance across all standards, with a small number of areas identified for further strengthening (e.g. forecasting consistency and longer-term financial planning).

findings.paper_title: Appendix L - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Inherited debt maturity profile weighted to later years with prohibitively high early redemption premiums limits refinancing flexibility
findings.detail: Rutland's debt was acquired when it became a Unitary Authority, inheriting a portion of Leicestershire County Council's debt. This resulted in a maturity profile heavily weighted to the latter years. Fixed rates and dates make early repayment extremely costly, eliminating practical refinancing options if rates or liquidity needs change.
findings.matters: Structural constraint on treasury flexibility. The council cannot refinance debt to respond to interest rate movements or operational needs without incurring prohibitive costs. This reduces financial agility and could increase borrowing costs if rates move unexpectedly.
findings.figures: Debt maturity profile shown in section 5.8.2; redemption premiums described as prohibitively high
findings.quote: However, the Council's debt position presents a challenge due to historic decisions taken when Rutland became a Unitary Authority. At that time, the Council was allocated a proportion of Leicestershire County Council's debt, resulting in a maturity profile that is heavily weighted towards the latter years. The fixed rates and maturity dates of this debt make early repayment difficult, as premiums for early redemption are prohibitively high.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H - Finance Risk Register
findings.headline: Government's Children's Social Care and SEND reforms create unfunded mandate risk due to uncertainties around scope, funding levels and timelines.
findings.detail: Two major government reforms (Families First for social care; national SEND reform) introduce uncertainty around scope, funding levels and implementation timelines. The council identifies this creates "risk of unfunded mandates and service disruption". The council has allocated contingency funding within the MTFS for Children's Social Care and is developing a DfE-approved Local SEND Reform Plan, but delivery risks remain around reform scope, conditions, capacity and transition costs.
findings.matters: Unfunded mandates represent direct cost pressures outside the council's control; uncertainty about funding and scope for two large demand-led services creates unquantified financial risk.
findings.figures: No specific forecast costs disclosed for reform implementation
findings.quote: Government's Families First reforms require councils to adopt new multi-disciplinary models and early intervention approaches. Uncertainty remains around the scope, funding, and timelines, creating risk of unfunded mandates and service disruption.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H - Finance Risk Register
findings.headline: Council holds accumulated £10.3m DSG (high-needs) deficit; while 90% government-funded from February 2026, residual risks remain around verification, reform approval and future-year support.
findings.detail: Rutland has an accumulated £10.3m and structural £5.0m DSG high-needs deficit. The Government's 9 February 2026 announcement introduced the High Needs Stability Grant funding 90% of verified deficit at 31 March 2026, with the council meeting the 10% residual share. However, the council acknowledges residual risks: eligibility/verification issues, reform plan approval, cash receipt timing (first payment expected Autumn 2026), and future-year support described as "proportionate, not unlimited".
findings.matters: The historic deficit is material; the 10% local share of £1m+ is substantial, and residual risks around verification, reform conditions, and ongoing support create financial uncertainty.
findings.figures: £10.3m accumulated deficit; £5.0m structural deficit; 90% government-funded; 10% local contribution required; first HNSG payment expected Autumn 2026
findings.quote: The Council holds a significant accumulated £10.3m and structural DSG (high-needs) deficit over £5.0m. The Government's announcement on 9 February 2026 introduced the High Needs Stability Grant (HNSG), which will fund 90% of the verified eligible deficit at 31 March 2026, with the remaining 10% met locally; proportionate support is also signalled for new deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, and the statutory override is extended to March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H - Finance Risk Register
findings.headline: Rutland council will cease to exist in its current form after March 2028 under planned Local Government Reorganisation, committing £2.5m from reserves for transition.
findings.detail: The council will transition to a new unitary authority post-March 2028. This creates risk to organisational capacity as resources divert to structural change, potentially impacting legacy project and business-as-usual service delivery. The shortened planning horizon may lead to decisions prioritising short-term gains over long-term sustainability. The council is committing £2.5m from reserves over two years for additional capacity in programme management, legal, commissioning and IT.
findings.matters: Fundamental structural change creates both immediate financial commitment (£2.5m reserves) and uncertainty about financial continuity and service delivery in the transitional authority.
findings.figures: £2.5m investment over two years from reserves for transition capacity; transition deadline March 2028
findings.quote: The Council is not expected to exist in its current form post March 2028, requiring a transition to a new authority. This creates a risk to organisational capacity, as resources will be diverted to manage structural change, potentially impacting the delivery of legacy projects and business-as-usual services.

findings.paper_title: Report No.04.2026 - Integrated Budget Plan (IBP) and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) - 2026.27 to 2028.29
findings.headline: Pay inflation assumptions of 3% annually and recruitment challenges create risk; sensitivity analysis shows a 10% pay variance = £1.61m budget impact.
findings.detail: The council assumes 3% annual pay awards, with the budget including costs for national awards and Employer National Insurance. However, the CFO identifies 'recruitment challenges' and 'workforce market conditions further heighten uncertainty.' The sensitivity analysis reveals that a 10% variance on pay costs (e.g., if the pay award settles at 4% instead of 3%) creates a £1.61m budget pressure. A 1% variance costs £230k. The council is in a tight labour market for key skills (especially social care caseworkers) where demand is outpacing supply.
findings.matters: Pay is a controllable cost only to a point. If recruitment and retention pressures force above-inflation pay awards, the council has limited mitigation short of cuts to staffing. With adult social care already under demand pressure and SEND reform requiring additional casework capacity, the council is vulnerable to pay-driven overspends it cannot easily absorb.
findings.figures: 3% pay award assumption for 2026/27–2028/29; 10% pay variance = £1.61m impact; 1% variance = £230k; employer NI and recruitment as additional pressures
findings.quote: Service areas such as social care and construction face cost increases of 5-15%, while pay inflation is rising due to national awards and recruitment challenges...Pay Award – 10% [sensitivity impact] 1,610 [£000]...recruitment challenges [further heighten] uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: Report No.04.2026 - Integrated Budget Plan (IBP) and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) - 2026.27 to 2028.29
findings.headline: Usable reserves of £19.2m at 31 March 2027 are 'substantially committed' through to 2028/29, with only £3.9m unallocated and the General Fund minimum held at £3.0m.
findings.detail: The council holds total usable reserves of £19.2m at 31 March 2027, but the CFO states these are 'substantially committed to statutory and policy requirements through to 31 March 2028, leaving only a modest unallocated headroom of £3.9m.' The General Fund minimum is held at £3.0m (a prudent working balance), ring-fenced amounts are earmarked for specific risks (DSG, risk management, innovation), and much of the remainder is committed to funding planned capital investment and transformation. This leaves minimal buffer for unforeseen events.
findings.matters: A council holding 67% of its budget in reserves appears well-cushioned, but it is not: the CFO explicitly states 'The Council does not hold significant spare reserves; rather, our reserves are finite, purpose-bound and prudently deployed.' If any major pressure emerges (e.g., ASC overspend, grant clawback, capital scheme failure), the council would quickly deplete its flexibility.
findings.figures: Total usable reserves £19.2m at 31 March 2027; unallocated headroom £3.9m; General Fund minimum £3.0m; reserves as % of budget 67% (highest among CIPFA Nearest Neighbours); committed reserves through 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The Council's usable reserves at 31 March 2025 are substantially committed to statutory and policy requirements through to 31 March 2028, leaving only a modest unallocated headroom of £3.9m to support the revenue budget and treasury flexibility...The Council does not hold 'significant spare reserves'; rather, our reserves are finite, purpose-bound and prudently deployed to protect financial resilience while avoiding the use of reserves to fund day-to-day expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Report No.04.2026 - Integrated Budget Plan (IBP) and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) - 2026.27 to 2028.29
findings.headline: Council assumes 3.30% interest rate on cash balances in 2026/27 (generating £0.7m additional income), explicitly flagged as 'sensitive to market volatility'.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumes 3.30% interest receipts, falling to 3.25% in subsequent years. This generates £0.7m additional income over current-year expectations. However, the CFO specifically flags: 'financial assumptions linked to interest receipts and cash flow profiling are sensitive to market volatility and increased accuracy of the timing of capital schemes.' If the Bank of England cuts rates materially below 3.3%, the council loses this income and faces a budget shortfall.
findings.matters: With already tight margins (£6.1m of planned savings from a £95.8m budget) and constrained reserves, a 0.5% drop in interest rates would cost ~£250k and force further emergency savings. The CFO's explicit warning signals that this assumption is not robust—it depends on rates remaining at current levels, which is not guaranteed.
findings.figures: 3.30% interest rate assumed 2026/27; 3.25% in 2027/28 and 2028/29; £0.7m additional income from higher-than-forecast rates; 1% rate change = £500k budget impact
findings.quote: The Council is expecting to generate additional income of £1.3m in relation to fees and charges compared to current year...£0.7m interest receipts on cash balances as rates have remained higher than previously forecast...These dependencies increase the likelihood of slippage or under-delivery, requiring close monitoring and contingency planning to maintain overall financial resilience...financial assumptions linked to interest receipts and cash flow profiling are sensitive to market volatility.

findings.paper_title: Report No.04.2026 - Integrated Budget Plan (IBP) and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) - 2026.27 to 2028.29
findings.headline: Adult Social Care carries a £1.5m pressure from 2025/26 and faces 6% demand growth; the CFO warns of 'higher-than-budgeted average costs per package' and risk of short-term exposure.
findings.detail: The ASC budget faces £1.5m carried-forward pressure, with an additional £0.5m investment proposed despite savings. Rutland's population aged 65+ is now 27.1% with a forecast 23.8% increase in the over-75 population by 2030. The CFO explicitly states: 'Individual placements can be extremely expensive...Current trends show higher-than-budgeted average costs per package, adding to in-year pressures.' Cost control measures (contract compliance, block bed procurement) may take time to deliver, leaving short-term exposure.
findings.matters: This is a non-discretionary, open-ended budget in a council with a 27% elderly population and worsening age profile. If placement costs continue to rise faster than inflation, the council will face uncontrollable overspends that will consume reserves or force service cuts elsewhere. The CFO's warning about timing of mitigation measures signals active risk management but also acknowledgment of current loss of control.
findings.figures: £1.5m pressure carried from 2025/26; £0.5m additional investment proposed; 27.1% of population aged 65+; 23.8% forecast increase in over-75 population by 2030; 6% demand growth assumption in 2026/27
findings.quote: For the Council the primary risk is the volatility of demand and cost pressures, which remain difficult to predict. Individual placements can be extremely expensive, and even small increases in service users or complexity of care can create significant financial strain. Current trends show higher-than-budgeted average costs per package, adding to in-year pressures.

findings.paper_title: Report No.04.2026 - Integrated Budget Plan (IBP) and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) - 2026.27 to 2028.29
findings.headline: The Council plans £4.8m savings in 2026/27 rising to £6.9m by 2028/29, with the CFO flagging 'Red and Amber rated risk savings' constrained by factors outside Council control.
findings.detail: The savings programme spans demand management (behavioural change, prevention measures), commissioning efficiencies, partnership-dependent redesigns (e.g., health & care hub), and income generation (interest receipts, fees). The CFO explicitly identifies that many savings 'rely on factors outside direct Council control or involve significant implementation uncertainty' and warns 'there is a risk around capacity and pace to deliver the full package.' Individual placements in social care can be extremely expensive, and even small increases in service users may offset planned savings.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has genuine control over its costs or whether delivery depends on external partners and unproven behavioural assumptions. If £6.9m of savings (from a £95.8m gross budget) slip, the council has limited headroom and would be forced to either cut services or draw reserves faster than planned.
findings.figures: £4.8m savings in 2026/27; £6.9m by 2028/29; £6.1m total savings + income generation required within £95.8m gross budget; CFO rates some savings as Red and Amber risk
findings.quote: The Red and Amber rated risk savings shown in Appendix B are constrained by the risk nature of several savings actions, which rely on factors outside direct Council control or involve significant implementation uncertainty. Demand management and prevention strategies depend on behavioural and demographic changes that may not materialise as planned, while initiatives such as health & care hub redesign require partnership working.

findings.paper_title: Report No.04.2026 - Integrated Budget Plan (IBP) and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) - 2026.27 to 2028.29
findings.headline: DSG high-needs deficit of £10.0m will be funded 90% nationally and 10% from council reserves, with the grant phased and conditional on a Reform Plan.
findings.detail: Rutland has accumulated a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of approximately £10.0m by 31 March 2026, driven by SEND demand growth of 16% since 2023. The Government's High Needs Stability Grant will cover 90% (around £9.3m), with the Council meeting the remaining 10% from the earmarked DSG Risk Reserve. The grant is cash-backed but phased, with the first payment expected in Autumn 2026, and continued support in 2026/27 and 2027/28 is proportionate, not unlimited.
findings.matters: This shows a persistent structural deficit in a ring-fenced service, evidencing either demand-management failure or systematic underfunding of SEND. The new arrangement is conditional on the Council executing a DfE Reform Plan—a compliance obligation. The phased cash receipt also introduces treasury timing risk that wasn't present when the council was cash-flowing the deficit.
findings.figures: £10.0m accumulated deficit at 31 March 2026; £9.3m (90%) funded by HNSG; £1.0m (10%) from Risk Reserve; SEND demand grew 16% since 2023; proportionate support signalled for 2026/27–2027/28
findings.quote: Rutland continues to carry a significant DSG (high-needs) deficit driven by sustained demand growth and cost inflation. The accumulated balance is forecast to reach c.£10.0m by 31 March 2026...On 9 February 2026, Government confirmed the High Needs Stability Grant (HNSG): 90% of each authority's verified eligible DSG deficit at 31 March 2026 will be funded nationally, with the remaining 10% met locally, subject to an approved DSG Reform Plan.

findings.paper_title: Report No.04.2026 - Integrated Budget Plan (IBP) and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) - 2026.27 to 2028.29
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 has swung from an anticipated £1.3m gain to a 19.9% funding loss.
findings.detail: The Government's funding formula was revised in late November 2025, reversing the summer consultation outcome. For Rutland, this triggered a £3.7m loss in retained business rates due to the baseline reset. The Council's general grant allocation per dwelling is now £641.40 in 2026/27, falling to £546.11 by 2028/29, compared to the national average of £1,426.44 rising to £1,468.91—a cumulative loss of £359 per dwelling by the end of the MTFS period.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial resilience needs to know that government funding has collapsed and cannot be recovered. The council is forced to rely on Council Tax for 81% of Core Spending Power by 2028/29 (vs. the national 55%), concentrating revenue risk on a single, politically constrained source.
findings.figures: 19.9% funding loss; £3.7m loss in retained business rates; grant allocation falling from £641.40 to £546.11 per dwelling; national average £1,426.44 rising to £1,468.91
findings.quote: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 is a major reform of how central government funding is allocated to English local authorities, to be implemented from April 2026...However, following a delay, brought about by ministerial changes, the results of the consultation were published as part of the Local Government Policy Statement in late November 2025. This revealed significant and fundamental changes to the funding formula that had been launched in the summer. For the Council this turned an estimated 6.4% funding gain into a 19.9% funding loss.

findings.paper_title: Appendix M - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Ashwell property portfolio disposal due to flooding and deterioration indicates asset quality issues
findings.detail: Annex A asset management strategy table shows Ashwell Business Units marked for DISPOSE across all years because 'Buildings in poor condition and not economic to invest. Flooding.' Ashwell Cottage also marked for disposal with septic tank and access issues. These represent portfolio liabilities rather than productive assets, requiring revenue spend for management rather than generating returns.
findings.matters: Portfolio contains non-performing assets requiring disposal; flooding risk indicates environmental/climate vulnerability of remaining property holdings and historical management gaps.
findings.figures: Ashwell Business Units and Cottage scheduled for disposal; disposal planned early 2026 for Business Units via auction
findings.quote: Buildings in poor condition and not economic to invest. Flooding. Option for BNG offset – tbc. If not suitable, then will auction early 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix M - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Meditech facility expanded scope (£4.3m commitment) still in business case development stage
findings.detail: Section 4.4.5 notes the Meditech facility, part of the £23m Levelling Up Fund programme, was originally designed for research and development. 'Cabinet has asked officers to develop a full business case for an enhanced scope, which will be reported separately.' Design work identified opportunity to elevate to 'state-of-the-art health-tech hub' meeting 'future clinical and sustainability standards.' No finalised scope or costs provided.
findings.matters: Major capital commitment (£4.3m from LUF) with scope and costs still being refined creates delivery risk, cost uncertainty, and potential for scope creep and overspend.
findings.figures: £4.3m LUF allocation; scope enhancement under development
findings.quote: Cabinet has asked officers to develop a full business case for an enhanced scope, which will be reported separately. This will ensure the facility meets future clinical and sustainability standards while delivering long-term benefits for Rutland.

findings.paper_title: Appendix M - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Limited capital assets available for sale significantly constrains traditional capital receipts funding route
findings.detail: Section 5.1 explicitly states 'The Council has limited capital assets which it could sell and use receipts to reinvest.' Annex A asset management table reinforces this: Ashwell Business Units and Cottage are marked for disposal due to poor condition and flooding (not sale for reinvestment value), while key operational properties like Catmose House and Museum are HOLD positions with maintenance bills rather than profit centres.
findings.matters: Limited assets for sale constrains capital funding flexibility and increases reliance on grants or new borrowing. Disposals driven by liability management rather than generating reinvestment capital.
findings.figures: Ashwell Business Units: flooding and poor condition; Catmose House: £3.5m condition survey over 5 years; Museum: £2.1m over 5 years
findings.quote: The Council has limited capital assets which it could sell and use receipts to reinvest

findings.paper_title: Appendix M - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council servicing £14m debt at £1.7m per annum cost constrains borrowing capacity
findings.detail: Section 5.1 states existing debt position and annual servicing obligation. This is a recurring revenue commitment that reduces available resources for new capital investment and limits headroom for additional prudential borrowing.
findings.matters: Annual debt service of £1.7m on £14m is a material and fixed revenue commitment; any new borrowing increases this burden and reduces financial flexibility during budget pressures.
findings.figures: £14m total debt; £1.7m per annum servicing cost
findings.quote: The Council is currently servicing debt of c£14m, the current cost of servicing this debt is £1.7m per annum

findings.paper_title: Appendix M - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation introduces structural governance risk requiring shadow authority consent for high-value capital decisions
findings.detail: Section 3.1 notes the transition to a new unitary authority introduces 'significant financial and operational challenges' requiring careful capital planning. Section 24-style controls may require consent from the shadow authority for high-value commitments. Risk mitigation includes a Corporate Programme Board overseeing all LGR and legacy projects, with Audit & Risk Committee maintaining oversight. Key risks identified: capacity constraints, timescale uncertainty, and short-term decision-making.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation uncertainty affects capital planning assumptions, borrowing approvals, and asset valuations. Shadow authority controls create potential approval delays and restrict Rutland's autonomous capital decision-making during MTFS period.
findings.figures: MTFS period 2026/27-2028/29; vesting date unspecified
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) introduces significant financial and operational challenges that will shape Rutland's capital investment approach over the Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix I - Reserves Strategy + Policy
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 includes grant reductions of £1.2m across MTFS period despite three-year certainty
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review implementation from April 2026 provides three-year funding certainty, but the revised settlement includes grant reductions totalling £1.2m across the MTFS period. This reinforces pressure on the council's financial position and underlines the need for continued transformation and robust savings delivery.
findings.matters: Grant reductions lock in additional funding pressure; while certainty is positive, the direction is negative and narrows financial options available to the council
findings.figures: Grant reductions: £1.2m across MTFS period
findings.quote: the revised settlement includes grant reductions of £1.2m across the MTFS period, increasing pressure on the Council's financial position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix I - Reserves Strategy + Policy
findings.headline: Adults & Health overspend identified in Q2 outturn; demand-led budget pressures continuing to materialise
findings.detail: The Q2 forecast shows an overall position masked by a significant overspend in Adults & Health, only mitigated by savings elsewhere (waste, vacancies, highways). The strategy notes risks remain in relation to demand-led budgets, with vacancy levels presenting concurrent management risks.
findings.matters: Demand pressures on adult social care are materializing in-year despite budget planning; this is the most volatile and difficult area for councils to control, suggesting budget assumptions are proving optimistic
findings.figures: Q2 overspend: unspecified but described as significant; largely offset by other savings
findings.quote: This masks a significant overspend in Adults & Health. This position is mitigated by savings in waste disposal and management, vacancy savings, Highways & Transport Services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix I - Reserves Strategy + Policy
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation creates structural uncertainty; council "highly likely" to not exist in current form beyond 2028
findings.detail: The recent White Paper on Local Government Reorganisation introduces significant uncertainty to all planning. The council notes it is "now highly likely that Rutland County Council will not exist in its current form beyond 2028." This structural uncertainty extends through the MTFS period and undermines assumptions about continuity of service delivery and financial management.
findings.matters: Fundamental uncertainty about the council's existence and structure in current form creates risk that strategic plans cannot be executed as assumed; affects repayment capacity and ongoing operations
findings.figures: Reorganisation deadline: beyond 2028; MTFS period: 2026/27-2028/29
findings.quote: The recent White Paper on Local Government Reorganisation introduces significant uncertainty, as it is now highly likely that Rutland County Council will not exist in its current form beyond 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix I - Reserves Strategy + Policy
findings.headline: Total usable reserves declining 49% from £25.7m to £13.2m over three years; only £3.9m unallocated headroom
findings.detail: The chart shows reserve balances declining from an estimated £25.7m in 2025/26 to £13.2m by 2028/29. More critically, the council identifies that usable reserves at 31 March 2025 are substantially committed to statutory and policy requirements through to 31 March 2028, leaving only a modest £3.9m unallocated headroom to support the revenue budget and treasury flexibility.
findings.matters: Sharp reserve decline and low unallocated headroom significantly constrains council flexibility to manage unexpected events or pressures; indicates limited financial cushion despite absolute reserve size
findings.figures: Total reserves: £25.7m (2025/26) declining to £13.2m (2028/29); unallocated headroom: £3.9m
findings.quote: leaving only a modest unallocated headroom of £3.9m to support the revenue budget and treasury flexibility.

findings.paper_title: Appendix I - Reserves Strategy + Policy
findings.headline: Government grant covers 90% of DSG deficit; council applying £2.4m local contribution from Risk Reserve
findings.detail: The High Needs Stability Grant announced February 2026 will fund 90% of Rutland's verified DSG deficit at 31 March 2026. The council is drawing £2.4m from its Risk Reserve to meet the required 10% local contribution. This represents a major shift from previous arrangements and materially reduces the single largest risk to the medium-term financial strategy.
findings.matters: Large drawdown from Risk Reserve commits a material portion of risk mitigation funds; lenders need to know council resilience has improved due to external funding rather than internal financial performance
findings.figures: £2.4m local contribution; 90% government funding; DSG "override" deficit balance (10,329) reducing to (5,626) by 2026/27
findings.quote: The governments announcement on High Needs Stability Grant is expected to fund 90% of Rutland's verified DSG deficit at 31 March 2026, materially reducing the single largest risk to the MTFS and improving overall resilience.

findings.paper_title: Report No.124.2025 - Review of Reserves Strategy to Mitigate Risk
findings.headline: DSG deficit risk rated as HIGH with no mitigation beyond awaiting government action
findings.detail: The council's own risk register rates the DSG deficit risk as 'High' with residual risk also rated 'High'. The mitigation offered is only to await government announcements on reform and funding. The council notes it is 'cash flowing' DSG expenditure that it cannot recover, and this will severely impair financial resilience if government does not provide a solution.
findings.matters: A High-rated risk with no actionable mitigation indicates the council has limited ability to manage this threat independently. The entire resolution depends on decisions by the Department for Education and the government, which have not yet been made.
findings.figures: Risk 2 rated High; no mitigation available beyond awaiting government reform announcements expected in early 2026
findings.quote: Without a known solution this is a significant risk that could expose, and dramatically reduce, the Council's financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: Report No.124.2025 - Review of Reserves Strategy to Mitigate Risk
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation: Rutland County Council may cease to exist in its current form after 2028
findings.detail: A government white paper on Local Government Reorganisation creates significant uncertainty. The council believes it is certain that Rutland County Council will not exist in its present form post-2028. The council notes that 'further considerations are required with regards to the financial risk of Local Government Reorganisation' but these have not yet been undertaken or incorporated into the financial strategy.
findings.matters: If the council is reorganised or merged, its financial commitments, pension liabilities, and accumulated deficits transfer to a successor body. This creates uncertainty about how debts will be settled and whether reserve policies will be honoured. A lender needs to understand the client may not exist as a borrowing entity within the medium term.
findings.figures: Uncertainty expected to be resolved post-2028
findings.quote: the recent white paper on Local Government Reorganisation creates further significant uncertainty as it appears certain that Rutland County Council will not exist in its present form post 2028.

findings.paper_title: Report No.124.2025 - Review of Reserves Strategy to Mitigate Risk
findings.headline: Substantial government funding reform expected but not yet confirmed, creating medium-term budget uncertainty
findings.detail: The council states that Local Government Funding Reforms will increase uncertainty of future funding levels. Further details are expected as part of the Local Government Finance Settlement in early 2026. Until this is published, the council cannot finalise its medium-term budget assumptions and reserves strategy.
findings.matters: Government funding is the primary source of council revenue. Uncertainty about funding levels prevents the council from finalising its financial plan with confidence. This is a material risk to the forward-looking financial position.
findings.figures: No figures provided; settlement expected early 2026
findings.quote: Local Government Funding Reforms increase the uncertainty of future funding levels whilst Local Government continues to face challenges of rising demand, expectations from the public and government, and rising costs of service delivery that outstrip the funding available.

findings.paper_title: Report No.124.2025 - Review of Reserves Strategy to Mitigate Risk
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability Strategy Reserve completely drawn by 2027/28, leaving no buffer for savings delivery failure
findings.detail: The council is using a dedicated reserve of £2m to cover the risk that planned savings will not be delivered on time or in full. This reserve is projected to reach zero by 2027/28. If substantial savings fail to materialise before then, the council will have no contingency and will need to draw on the general reserve or make emergency cuts.
findings.matters: This reveals that the council's financial plan is fragile and dependent on execution. If transformation programmes slip or savings cannot be achieved, the council will rapidly exhaust its buffers and face forced service reductions or breaches of prudential borrowing rules.
findings.figures: Financial Sustainability Strategy Reserve: March 2025 £2.0m; March 2026 £2.0m; March 2027 £0.411m; March 2028 £0m
findings.quote: This position is reliant on the delivery of saving plans. Therefore, this reserve is used to mitigate the risk of delivering the savings on time and to value and will therefore act as a Budget Risk Reserve.

findings.paper_title: Report No.124.2025 - Review of Reserves Strategy to Mitigate Risk
findings.headline: Total usable reserves declining from £24.4m to £16.2m over the four-year strategy period
findings.detail: The council's total reserves are projected to fall from £24.4m in March 2025 to £16.2m by March 2028. This decline is driven by planned use of the Financial Sustainability Strategy Reserve (which goes to zero by 2027/28) and drawdown of the Innovation Fund. The council acknowledges that recovery of these reserves depends on successful delivery of savings plans.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's capacity to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. By 2027/28, the council will have only the minimum £3m general fund plus risk reserves, with no strategic flexibility fund remaining.
findings.quote: The chart shows a reduction in the reserve balances from an estimated £22.9m to £15.1m over the period.

findings.paper_title: Report No.124.2025 - Review of Reserves Strategy to Mitigate Risk
findings.headline: DSG deficit projected to exceed the entire reserves balance by 2027/28 if government does not fund it
findings.detail: The accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is growing and the council has no certainty on government funding to cover it. The document shows in a chart that the projected deficit will exceed all council reserves by 2027/28. The government has announced reform plans but has not committed to funding the accumulated historic deficit. If the council must fund this from general reserves, its financial resilience will be severely impaired.
findings.matters: This represents an existential risk to the council's financial position. A lender needs to understand that without a government solution, the council's entire reserve cushion could be consumed by a single unfunded liability, leaving no capacity to manage other financial shocks.
findings.figures: Deficit expected to be negative £10m by end of 2025/26; chart shows deficit exceeds all reserves by 2027/28
findings.quote: The point the deficit exceeds all Council reserves being 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Report No.119.2025 - The Auditors Annual Audit Report 24.25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Audit and Risk Committee does not receive a formal copy of the Corporate Risk Register; oversight relies on verbal updates.
findings.detail: The audit identifies a governance gap: the Audit and Risk Committee receives verbal updates on the Corporate Risk Register rather than formal written copies. This limits transparent scrutiny of documented risks and means risks are not available as public documents in committee papers. While the audit rates this as adequate arrangements with opportunity for improvement (not a significant weakness), it signals a gap in governance transparency.
findings.matters: Risk registers are a key control for boards and audit committees. Relying on verbal updates rather than formal documentation reduces accountability and makes it harder for members to challenge risk assessments or track changes over time.
findings.figures: 18 financial risks identified in budget setting; ongoing Corporate Risk Register maintained but not formally disclosed to committee
findings.quote: The Audit and Risk Committee receive regular verbal updates on the Corporate Risk register, but as a result, the risk register is not available as a public document as part of the committee papers.

findings.paper_title: Report No.119.2025 - The Auditors Annual Audit Report 24.25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Service performance gaps are widening: housing delivery 54 vs 123 target; EHCP statutory compliance 26% vs 90% target; adult care reviews 45% vs 80% target.
findings.detail: The November 2024 Six-Month Progress Report (the latest available as of the audit date) showed material underperformance across statutory services. Housing delivery achieved only 44% of target. EHCP assessment timeliness is particularly weak at 26%, well below the 90% target and the 20-week statutory deadline. Adult social care reviews hit only 45% of target. These gaps are highlighted in the audit as areas requiring member challenge and corrective action.
findings.matters: These performance gaps in demand-driven services signal capacity or process issues. Weak EHCP assessment performance feeds directly into the DSG deficit problem (more assessments completed = more children into costly placements). Housing shortfall and care review backlogs indicate service stress.
findings.figures: Housing delivery 54 vs target 123; temporary accommodation 17 vs target 6; EHCP assessments 26% on time vs 90% target; adult care reviews 45% on time vs 80% target
findings.quote: Housing delivery recorded 54 new homes against a target of 123, and the number of households in temporary accommodation averaged 17 compared to a target of six. In Children's Services, 26% of EHCP assessments were completed within the 20-week statutory timescale against a 90% target. In Adults, 45% of care and support reviews were completed on time against an 80% target.

findings.paper_title: Report No.119.2025 - The Auditors Annual Audit Report 24.25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery remains significantly below budget: £6.8m spent against £19.94m budget in 2024/25, a £13.1m variance.
findings.detail: Capital spending has consistently underperformed against budget. In 2024/25, only £6.8m was spent against a revised budget of £19.94m. While Cabinet reports provide explanations for slippage (including Levelling Up projects and waste vehicle timing), the persistent large variance raises questions about project delivery capability and phasing assumptions in future budgets.
findings.matters: Consistent capital underspend suggests either poor planning discipline or delivery challenges. This matters for infrastructure investment assumptions and the council's ability to execute its £43.6m three-year capital plan.
findings.figures: 2024/25 capital expenditure £6.8m against revised budget £19.94m (variance £13.1m); planned 3-year investment £43.60m
findings.quote: The 2024/25 budget was £19.94m, with expenditure of £6.8m. The report sets out changes since the previous quarter and also explains the reasons for slippage. The explanations are reasonable.

findings.paper_title: Report No.119.2025 - The Auditors Annual Audit Report 24.25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Medium-term financial pressures rising: £6.6m in 2025/26 escalating to £14.63m by 2027/28, with £0.44m of savings targets still unmitigated (red-rated) as of Q1 2025/26.
findings.detail: The MTFS shows material and growing budget pressures. While Q1 2025/26 shows £3.12m of identified savings exceeding the £2.24m requirement, the savings tracker records £0.44m as red-rated with unmitigated shortfalls. The audit notes the chief finance officer judged the 2025/26 budget as "realistic and deliverable, albeit challenging". These are structural pressures requiring continued focus on delivery.
findings.matters: The escalating pressure from £6.6m to £14.63m over three years shows fiscal headroom is tightening. The existence of red-rated savings (unmitigated shortfalls) signals execution risk in the council's savings delivery plan.
findings.figures: 2025/26 pressures £6.6m; 2027/28 pressures £14.63m; Q1 2025/26 red-rated shortfalls £0.44m; savings delivery in 2024/25 £1.13m in-year against £1.86m target
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) identifies additional budget pressures of £6.60m in 2025/26, rising to £14.63m by 2027/28, which are balanced through identified solutions. £0.44m were Red-rated (including £0.40m unmitigated shortfalls).

findings.paper_title: Report No.119.2025 - The Auditors Annual Audit Report 24.25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Investment income boost masked underlying spending pressures in 2024/25; forecast investment income shortfall of £0.55m in 2025/26 due to DSG cash funding.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 outturn showed a £0.2m underspend, but this was achieved only through £0.845m of additional investment income, grant income, waste disposal savings, and planning fees offsetting service overspends in Adult Social Care and Home to School Transport. Critically, the council is losing investment income because it must use cash reserves to fund the DSG deficit: foregone interest forecast at £0.55m in 2025/26 (up from £0.22m in 2024/25). This reduces available reserves and borrowing capacity.
findings.matters: One-off savings masking structural overspends are a warning sign. The widening investment income shortfall shows the DSG deficit is consuming both reserves and the income yield on those reserves, a double drag on financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 2024/25 investment income boost £0.845m; forecast investment income loss 2025/26 £0.55m (compared to £0.22m in 2024/25)
findings.quote: This was supported by £0.85m of additional investment income, grant income, and savings in waste disposal and planning fees, which offset overspends in Adult Social Care and Home to School Transport. The Council estimates that foregone interest will cost £0.55m in 2025/26, compared to £0.22m in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Report No.119.2025 - The Auditors Annual Audit Report 24.25 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit worsening: cumulative DSG deficit reached £5.916m and forecast to reach at least £9.60m by March 2026.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 DSG overspend was £2.931m, significantly higher than the £1.1m estimated when the budget was set. Demand for Education, Health and Care Plans has increased 69% since 2020, with higher cost placements in specialist provision and rising unit costs driving the increase. The High Needs Block is the main area of risk. Although the statutory override defers impact on the General Fund until March 2026 (likely extended to March 2028), the position presents a material medium-term risk to financial sustainability if not addressed.
findings.matters: A growing unfunded liability in a statutory service creates long-term financial strain and limits discretionary spending capacity. Lenders need to understand whether this trajectory can be halted before the statutory override expires.
findings.figures: 2024/25 overspend £2.931m; cumulative deficit £5.916m; forecast at least £9.60m by March 2026; demand for EHCPs up 69% since 2020
findings.quote: The 2024/25 DSG overspent by £2.93m, against an estimated deficit of £1.1m when the budget was set, increasing the cumulative deficit to £5.92m. The High Needs Block is the main area of risk, with demand for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCP) (up 69% since 2020), higher cost placements in specialist provision, and rising unit costs contributing to the deficit.
